title: NEB Class 11 Biology — Vegetation — 2025
origin: curated NEB-pattern set covering every topic of the class-11 vegetation unit

questions.question: Define vegetation and describe the main types of vegetation found in Nepal.
questions.solution:
Vegetation means the plant cover of a region — the assemblage of plant communities growing there naturally, as distinct from a single flora or species list.
Nepal's vegetation follows altitude and rainfall: tropical and subtropical sal and mixed hardwood forests in the Terai and inner Terai up to about 1,000 m; temperate forests of oak, rhododendron, chestnut and alder from about 1,000–3,000 m; coniferous forests of pine, fir, spruce and juniper with birch higher up; alpine shrubs, meadows and cushion plants above the treeline; and almost no vegetation on the high Himalaya, where only mosses, lichens and snow algae survive.

questions.question: Differentiate in-situ from ex-situ conservation and give two examples of each in Nepal.
questions.solution:
In-situ conservation protects species in their natural habitat, where they continue to evolve with the ecosystem: national parks and wildlife reserves (Chitwan National Park, Sagarmatha National Park), conservation areas and Ramsar sites, plus community forests and sacred groves.
Ex-situ conservation keeps species outside their habitat when the wild population is too small or its habitat is gone: botanical gardens (Godavari, Mahendra Ratna), seed banks, tissue-culture and zoo collections and captive breeding. In-situ is preferred because it preserves the whole community, while ex-situ is a safety net and a source of material for reintroduction.

questions.question: Explain how human activities affect natural vegetation and suggest three measures to reduce the damage.
questions.solution:
People clear forest for farmland, settlements, roads and hydropower, cut trees for fuelwood and timber, overgraze pastures, set fires and quarry hillsides. Plantations of a single species replace mixed forest, invasive species such as Mikania and Lantana spread, and pollution plus climate change shift the tree line. The result is deforestation, soil erosion and landslides, drying of springs, loss of habitat and extinction of species.
Measures: protect remaining forest through community forestry and strict law enforcement, promote fuel alternatives, terrace farming, agroforestry and reforestation with native species, and plan roads and dams with environmental impact assessment and habitat corridors.

questions.question: Which forest type dominates the Terai region of Nepal and which dominates the upper temperate zone?
questions.solution:
The Terai, below about 1,000 m with high rainfall and warm temperature, carries tropical and subtropical deciduous forest dominated by sal (Shorea robusta) with sissoo, khair and tall grasses.
The upper temperate zone, roughly 2,000–3,000 m, carries broad-leaved temperate forest of oak, rhododendron and laurel, passing into conifers — pine, fir, spruce and hemlock — and finally birch and juniper near the treeline.

questions.question: Why is Nepal rich in floral diversity? Mention the role of protected areas in conserving vegetation.
questions.solution:
Nepal spans only about 147,000 km² but rises from 60 m to 8,848 m, so it carries tropical, subtropical, temperate, subalpine and alpine climates within short distances; the monsoon adds a strong east–west rainfall gradient, and varied geology and soils add further niches. This is why the country holds a large share of the Himalayan flora, including many endemic and medicinal plants.
Protected areas conserve whole vegetation types and their successions, keep habitats large enough for wildlife, protect watersheds and gene pools, and support research, tourism and local livelihoods; buffer zones and community forests extend protection beyond park boundaries.
